title: Birria de Res
subtitle: slow-braised beef in dried chilli broth with consomme for dipping
excerpt: Birria de res is a rich, deeply spiced beef braise from Jalisco. The cooking liquid becomes a flavourful consomme served alongside for dipping. It takes time but very little active effort.
sourceNotes: Birria originated in the Mexican state of Jalisco, where it was traditionally made with goat. Beef birria became the popular variation across northern Mexico and Mexican communities in the United States, where it gained worldwide attention in the 2010s through birria tacos dipped in the cooking consomme.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the beef and consomme separately for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Scale up easily for a crowd. The consomme improves with more bones added.

glossaryTerms.definition: A clarified, intensely flavoured broth. In birria, the cooking liquid from the beef and chillies is served as a dipping broth alongside the filled tacos.

content.text: This recipe serves 6 and takes around 3 hours and 30 minutes in total, though most of that is hands-off braising time. The beef cooks slowly in a sauce of toasted dried chillies and aromatics until it is tender enough to pull apart with a fork. The braising liquid becomes a rich
served alongside for dipping the filled tacos.

Toasting the dried chillies before soaking them is not optional. A dry pan over a medium heat for 30 seconds per side wakes up the oils and gives the broth its depth. Do not let them blacken or the broth will taste bitter. Soak the toasted chillies in boiling water for 20 minutes until completely soft before blending.

Heat a dry frying pan over a medium hob. Toast the ancho and guajillo chillies for 30 seconds each side until fragrant. Do not let them blacken. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water and soak for 20 minutes until completely soft.
Preheat the oven to 160C. Drain the soaked chillies and place them in a blender with the onion, garlic, tinned tomatoes, cinnamon stick and 300ml of water. Blend until completely smooth.

Heat the vegetable oil in a large casserole dish over a high hob. Season the beef pieces generously with salt. Brown the beef in batches for 2 to 3 minutes per side until deeply coloured. Do not crowd the pan. Remove and set aside.
Pour the blended chilli sauce into the casserole dish. Return all the browned beef to the dish. Add enough water to just cover the beef, around 500ml. Stir to combine.

Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, until the beef is completely tender and pulls apart easily. Check occasionally and add a splash of water if the liquid reduces too much.
Remove the beef and shred it with two forks. Taste the braising liquid and adjust the seasoning. This is your consomme. Ladle it into cups or small bowls for dipping.
Warm the corn tortillas over a dry pan or directly over a gas flame. Fill with the shredded beef, top with chopped coriander and a squeeze of lime. Serve with the consomme alongside for dipping.

attrs.cause: The dried chillies were toasted too long and scorched
attrs.fix: Toast chillies for no more than 30 seconds per side in a dry pan. They should darken slightly and smell toasty. If they blacken and smoke, discard them and start again as the bitterness will not cook out.

attrs.symptom: The beef is still tough after the full cooking time
attrs.cause: Chuck needs high internal moisture and consistent low heat to break down its connective tissue
attrs.fix: Return the dish to the oven for a further 30 to 45 minutes. Make sure the lid is tightly sealed so steam does not escape. If the beef sits above the liquid, add another 200ml of water before continuing.

attrs.symptom: The consomme is very thin and watery
attrs.cause: Too much water was added, or the lid was not sealed tightly and steam escaped
attrs.fix: After removing the beef, simmer the consomme uncovered on the hob over a medium heat for 10 to 15 minutes to concentrate the flavour. Taste and season again before serving.

content.text: Birria comes from the state of Jalisco in western Mexico. It started as a goat stew for celebrations and weddings. The beef version spread north and became a street food staple. Birria tacos dipped in consomme are now popular at food markets and restaurants around the world.
